paragraphs.text: Bembi et al. (2008) described glycogenosis type II as a progressive, debilitating and often fatal neuromuscular disorder. Its clinical phenotypes form a continuum that varies in which organs are involved, age at onset and severity. In the late-onset form, residual acid maltase activity is present in muscle (Mehler and DiMauro, 1977). Patients have progressive proximal muscle weakness, mainly of the pelvic girdle, and later develop respiratory insufficiency with diaphragmatic weakness (Trend et al., 1985; Laforet et al., 2000).

paragraphs.text: Makos et al. (1987) reported 3 sons of healthy, nonconsanguineous parents who developed progressive proximal muscle weakness secondary to alpha-glucosidase deficiency. Each brother developed a fusiform basilar artery aneurysm. In 2 brothers the aneurysm ruptured fatally, and in the third it was complicated by cerebellar infarction. In the surviving brother, similar glycogen deposition was shown in the smooth muscle of the superficial temporal artery.

There were 44 males and 43 females, the median age was 44 years, and 82 patients were Caucasian. Forty-six percent had 1 or more abnormalities, most often LVH by ECG (12%), a short PR interval (10%), and decreased ejection fraction (7%). Six patients had a left ventricular ejection fraction below 55% (range, 41-54%). Only 4 patients (5%) had an elevated left ventricular mass index on echocardiogram, all in the mild range, and the severe ventricular hypertrophy typical of infantile Pompe disease was not seen. Other findings included sinus tachycardia (5 of 84), prolonged QTc (3 of 84), left atrial enlargement (3 of 84), incomplete bundle branch block (2 of 84), and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome (2 of 84). No patient had atrioventricular block, right ventricular hypertrophy, or ventricular tachycardia. The authors noted that the abnormalities might be due to Pompe disease or to comorbid conditions.

paragraphs.text: Patient 1 of Herbert et al. (2019) was a Caucasian boy who presented at 5 months with delayed motor development and feeding difficulties. CK, ALT, and AST were elevated, and muscle fibers contained PAS-positive vacuoles. He had generalized hypotonia, head lag, myopathic facies, and hypertrophied calf muscles. EMG showed myotonic discharges, barium swallow showed aspiration, and he had obstructive and central apneas. paragraphs.text: Raben et al. (1998) generated mice homozygous for targeted disruption of the Gaa gene (6neo/6neo). The mice lacked enzyme activity, accumulated glycogen in cardiac and skeletal muscle lysosomes by 3 weeks of age, and had markedly reduced mobility and strength by 3.5 weeks. In a second model, mice with deletion of exon 6 (Delta6/Delta6) had unimpaired strength and mobility up to 6.5 months of age, although their biochemical and pathologic changes were indistinguishable from those of the 6neo/6neo mice.
